title: Higher Order Functions and Passing Functions as Arguments
summary: Uses Chrome DevTools and a small calculator to show that functions can be passed as arguments to other functions (higher order functions), which is exactly what addEventListener relies on. Ends with a challenge to complete a four-operation calculator and step through it in the debugger.

concepts.heading: Experimenting on a live page with DevTools
points: Right-click an element, choose Inspect, and the selected element is available in the console as $0.
Assigning to a property such as $0.innerHTML = "..." changes the text on the page instantly. Only the local copy in your browser changes; a reload restores the original from the server.
$0.addEventListener("click", function () { console.log(...) }) attaches a listener to a page you did not write, and clicking the element then logs to the console every time.

concepts.heading: addEventListener takes a function as input
points: The first input is the event type string; the second is the function to run once that event is detected.
The second input can be an anonymous function or a named function such as respondToClick.
Unlike earlier functions that receive strings or numbers, this one receives a function as data. The browser's own implementation is hidden, so the lecture rebuilds the same pattern with a calculator.

concepts.heading: Why pass a function: the calculator
points: A calculator(num1, num2) that hard-codes + must be edited to switch to *, which is clumsy.
Better: make small single-purpose functions (add, multiply, and later subtract, divide), each taking two numbers and returning a result.
Give calculator a third parameter, operator. Inside it, call operator(num1, num2) and return the result.

At the call site the operator argument is the function's name only, with no parentheses, e.g. calculator(4, 5, add) returns 9 and calculator(4, 5, multiply) returns 20. Passing the name hands over the function; parentheses would call it first and pass its result instead.

Trace of calculator(4, 5, multiply): 4 binds to num1, 5 to num2, the multiply function binds to operator; the body calls operator with the two numbers; its return value becomes calculator's return value.

concepts.heading: Higher order functions
points: A function that accepts another function as an argument (like calculator, and like addEventListener) is called a higher order function.
This is available in many modern languages (JavaScript, Swift, Pascal) but not all. It is used constantly in DOM scripting.

concepts.heading: Using the Chrome debugger
points: Type the keyword debugger in the console (Shift+Enter for a new line), then a call such as calculator(3, 4, multiply), and execution pauses in the Sources panel.
Use the step-into button (down arrow) to advance one call at a time. The scope panel shows num1 = 3, num2 = 4 and operator shown as a function (marked with f).
Stepping shows control enter calculator, jump into multiply, then return 12 back out through both functions.
Use this when code misbehaves, instead of simulating execution mentally, which can be wrong.

code_examples.caption: Passing functions into calculator (matches the reference repo)

task.name: Complete the four-operation calculator
task.starting_point: A calculator(num1, num2, operator) function plus add and multiply functions, in the console or a script file.
task.goal: Add divide and subtract so any of the four operations can be selected by passing a function to calculator.
steps: Write add, subtract, multiply and divide, each with two parameters and a return value.
Write calculator(num1, num2, operator) that returns operator(num1, num2).
Call it for each operation, passing the function by name (no parentheses), e.g. calculator(6, 3, subtract).
Use the debugger keyword and step-through to follow one call.
task.expected_result: Each call returns the right arithmetic result (e.g. 6 and 3 with subtract gives 3).
task.reference_repo_path: Section 18 - Advanced Javascript and DOM Manipulation/18.02 - Higher Order Functions and Passing Functions as Arguments/script.js

pitfalls: Writing calculator(4, 5, add()) which calls add immediately with undefined arguments and passes NaN or a result instead of a function.
Forgetting the return statement inside calculator, so it yields undefined.
(Extra) $0 only refers to the most recently inspected element, and edits made in DevTools vanish on reload.

playground.coverage: No playground lesson yet (section 18 has no playground file).
gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'Functions as values': tasks: (1) write add/subtract/multiply/divide, (2) write calculator taking an operator function, (3) pass an anonymous arrow function as operator, (4) predict outputs of calculator(4,5,add) vs calculator(4,5,add()), (5) write your own higher order function that calls a callback twice.
Interactive demo: pick an operator from a dropdown and see which function is passed, with a visual trace of the call stack mimicking the debugger steps.
